doc.title: James Moody — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Advice, listening and the record business
title: Becoming a soloist without knowing about practice
summary: He kept playing in the band without realizing one must practice until the Philadelphia remark about Sonny Rollins.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: Right. Right, right. So then after that initial solo experience on Emmanon, that -- did that pretty much establish you
as a soloist, then, within the band or did you have to wait a little while before you got some more experience?

No, I was playing in the band anyway and I wasn't playing anything. I was [scatting]. I mean, I -- I didn't, you know, know you were supposed to practice and you're supposed to play different things. I didn't know that.
How did you come on that knowledge? Did somebody show you that that's what you needed to do, or was that something you picked up from being around the other musicians?
Oh, don't you remember -- I told you -- remember yesterday when we were taking about the Phil Board [phonetic sp.] in Philly -­
-- the guy said, "Sonny Rollins [phonetic sp.] wrote this out for me." Wrote it out? I wonder what? And then 2 and 2 started clicking, said, "Oh, okay." I mean, you're supposed to do that.
'Cause it sounded from what you doing, like, in those '46 and '47, I mean '45 and '46 recordings that you'd already figured that out, it was still -­
